central_question: Why does a coffee cup stay hot even when the liquid is gone?
hook: You pour out your last drop of coffee, yet the mug still feels warm to the touch. How can an empty cup keep heat?
aha_moment: The ceramic wall stores a lot of thermal energy and, because it conducts heat slowly and is surrounded by trapped air, it releases that heat over minutes, keeping the surface warm.

story_arc.reveal: An empty mug still feels hot after the coffee is poured out.
required_facts: Coffee poured out, mug feels warm

story_arc.reveal: The mug’s material keeps the heat, but how?

story_arc.purpose: First reveal – conduction into the wall
story_arc.reveal: Heat from the coffee flows into the ceramic wall by conduction.
The wall’s mass and specific heat let it hold a lot of energy.

story_arc.purpose: Third reveal – low conductivity slows loss
story_arc.reveal: Ceramic conducts heat slowly, creating a high thermal resistance across its thickness.
required_facts: Thermal conductivity ~1 W/m·K, wall thickness ~5 mm

story_arc.reveal: It’s not steam keeping it warm; the solid wall is the source.

story_arc.purpose: Fourth reveal – outer surface loses heat mainly by convection
story_arc.reveal: Heat escapes through natural convection (h≈10 W/m²·K) and a tiny bit by radiation.

story_arc.purpose: Fifth reveal – trapped air in glaze adds insulation
story_arc.reveal: The glaze’s thin air layer further slows heat flow to the outside.
All these resistances give a cooling time of 10–20 minutes, enough to feel warm.

ending_payoff: When the last drop is gone, the mug’s wall is still a slow‑burning battery of heat, so touching it feels like a warm hug—proof that even an empty cup can surprise you with its hidden thermal memory.
